title: London, Past the Postcards
subtitle: Dawn on the river → Greenwich → Highgate
intro: The famous London at sunrise, before the city wakes up. Then two stories most tourists never hear. Saturday: the river at sunrise, a market the local people bought back, and a carpenter who beat the scientists in Greenwich. Sunday: the hill above London, with a huge old cemetery, and the place where a boy leaving London turned back.

dayGlance.title: Dawn on the river
dayGlance.sub: 7:00 Saturday. Walk from Big Ben to Tower Bridge. Breakfast at Borough Market.

dayGlance.title: Greenwich
dayGlance.sub: 10:25. Boat to Greenwich. The Painted Hall, the red ball at 1pm, and Harrison's clocks.

acts.label: Act 1 · Dawn on the river
acts.tagline: The famous London, before it wakes up.
acts.narrative:
Start on Westminster Bridge just after sunrise. Walk east along the river, in the morning light. Everyone has seen these places. So for each one, say one thing people don't know: the famous bell is cracked, the old London Bridge is in America, and the story of the ravens is not really old.

In the middle is Borough Market. You visit it twice: once while it's getting ready, and once when it's open. People have sold food here for 800 years. Parliament once closed it. The local people bought it back, and they still own it.

acts.label: Act 2 · Greenwich
acts.tagline: A carpenter, a clock, and the line that splits the world.
acts.narrative:
Take the boat down the river, and arrive at Greenwich from the water, the way it was meant to be seen. The Painted Hall was built as a dining room for old sailors. It was so grand that they didn't want to eat there.

Then walk up the hill for the main story. Sailors couldn't tell where they were at sea, and ships crashed. Parliament offered a big prize. The scientists looked at the stars. A carpenter built a clock. His clocks still work. And you finish standing on the line that splits the world into east and west.

acts.label: Act 3 · Highgate
acts.narrative:
Take the Northern line to Archway and go up the hill. In the 1800s, London had no more room for its dead, so they built this big cemetery. It became the most fashionable place to be buried.

Across the road is a park that a Lord Mayor gave to the public in 1889. That's where you tell the story the cemetery doesn't allow. Then walk down the hill to the stone from the story of Dick Whittington: a poor boy leaving London heard the bells and turned back. The real Whittington was rich, and there was no cat. But he gave all his money to the city.

kit: Phone or camera. No tripod at Borough Market or Highgate.
A power bank. Saturday is long: 7am to after 2pm.
A light jacket. It's about 12°C at 7am and 22°C in the afternoon.
Comfortable shoes. About 5 km of walking on Saturday, and Highgate is on a hill.
A bank card you can tap. It works on the tube and on the boat.
Tickets on your phone: Royal Observatory, Painted Hall, Highgate Cemetery.
preTrip: Book the Royal Observatory and the Painted Hall for Saturday.
Book your train home from Euston on Sunday, at about 4pm. Check for works on the line when you book.
If you want to be sure about filming, call Highgate: 020 8347 2472.
Charge everything on Friday night. You leave at about 6:30am.
goldenRule: Saturday has two fixed times: the 10:25 boat and the red ball at exactly 1:00. Plan everything else around them.

Tap your bank card. The red ball drops at exactly 1:00. It doesn't work in strong wind. Weather: some sun, 12°C in the morning, up to 22°C, dry.

days.planHeader: The hill above London · 10:00 AM – 2:45 PM

planNote.text: Take the Northern line to Archway. Then walk 15 to 20 minutes up the hill, or take a bus up Highgate Hill. Highgate Cemetery is open 10:00 to 5:00, last entry 4:30, £10. You can walk around both sides on your own. Filming for yourself is allowed, but no stories about ghosts or vampires inside. It's a real cemetery: if there is a funeral, move away. Archway to Euston is about 10 minutes on the Northern line. Book a train home for about 4pm. Weather: some sun, up to 21°C, dry.

planArrival.title: Home
planArrival.note: Archway station is at the bottom of the hill. Northern line to Euston, about 10 minutes. Train home at about 4pm.

westminster.name: Big Ben & the London Eye
westminster.angle: Big Ben is a cracked bell
westminster.story: You are on Westminster Bridge. On one side is Parliament with the famous clock tower. On the other side is the London Eye. Everyone knows this view. So tell people something they don't know: Big Ben is not the tower. It is the bell inside.
facts: The Parliament building is not as old as it looks. The old one burned down in 1834. For hundreds of years, the government recorded money on wooden sticks. They cut a notch in the stick for every payment. By 1834 nobody used these sticks any more, and there was a huge pile of them. Workers were told to burn them in the heating furnace under Parliament. They burned too many at once. The fire spread, and almost the whole building burned down.

The London Eye was built for the year 2000. At first, it was only allowed to stand for five years. It's still here, 26 years later. It has 32 capsules, one for each part of London. But the numbers go up to 33, because they skipped number 13.

routeCard.note: Westminster tube station is at the end of the bridge.

see: Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament
Westminster Bridge in the early light
planCard.todo: Be on the bridge at 7:00, just after sunrise. First film Parliament, then turn around for the London Eye. At 7:30, walk east along the river on the South Bank.

westminster.onCamera: This is Big Ben. Well, not exactly. Big Ben is not the tower. It's the name of the big bell inside it. The tower is called the Elizabeth Tower.
westminster.closeOnCamera: And the bell, Big Ben? It's cracked. It first rang in 1859. Two months later, it cracked, and it was silent for four years. Then they turned the bell a little and used a lighter hammer. The crack is still there today. So when you hear Big Ben, you are hearing a cracked bell.

st-pauls.name: Millennium Bridge & St Paul's
st-pauls.angle: A bridge that wobbled, a dome that survived
st-pauls.story: Stand at the south end of the Millennium Bridge. From here, the big dome of St Paul's Cathedral is right at the end of the bridge. Two stories here: a new bridge that had to close after two days, and an old cathedral that survived the bombs of the Second World War.
facts: The old St Paul's burned down in the Great Fire of London in 1666. A man called Christopher Wren designed the new one. It took 35 years to build. Wren lived long enough to see it finished. That almost never happened with a big cathedral.

In the Second World War, German planes bombed London. On the night of 29 December 1940, the streets around St Paul's were on fire. Churchill, the Prime Minister, said the cathedral must be saved. Volunteers stayed on the roof all night and put out the fire bombs. The next morning, a photo of the dome above the smoke became one of the most famous photos of the war.

routeCard.note: About 30 minutes' walk from Westminster Bridge, along the river.

see: Shakespeare's Globe, on the walk onwards
planCard.todo: Stand at the south end of the bridge, where the dome is right at the end. At 8:20, keep walking east along the river, past the Globe theatre.

st-pauls.onCamera: See that big dome at the end of the bridge? That's St Paul's Cathedral. In 1940, everything around it was on fire. And it survived.
st-pauls.closeOnCamera: And this bridge I'm standing on? It opened in June 2000. Two days later, it had to close. So many people walked on it that it started to swing from side to side. People walked in step with the swing, and that made it worse. It took almost two years to fix. Londoners still call it the Wobbly Bridge.

borough-setup.name: Borough Market — the set-up
borough-setup.angle: The market the people bought back
borough-setup.story: Come before the market opens. You can see the traders bringing in food and building their stalls. This is a good moment for the market's big story: Parliament once closed it, and the local people bought it back.
facts: Borough Market says it started in the year 1014, maybe even earlier. We know for sure that people were trading here in the 1100s. It's one of the oldest food markets in London.

Why here? For hundreds of years, London Bridge was the only bridge across the river in central London. The next one was Westminster Bridge, where we started this morning. It opened in 1750. So all the food coming into London from the south came this way. And the market grew right here, where all the carts passed.

routeCard.note: You can film for yourself without asking. But no tripod, and security may ask what you are filming.

planCard.todo: Stay on the streets that go through the market: Stoney Street and Bedale Street. Ask the traders before you film them. They are working, not selling yet.

borough-setup.onCamera: It's not even nine o'clock, and this market is getting ready for the day. People have been selling food here for about 800 years.
borough-setup.closeOnCamera: Here's my favourite part. In the 1750s, the market blocked the road so badly that Parliament closed it down. But the local people didn't want to lose it. They collected six thousand pounds. Today that's about a million. They bought a piece of land, and they got a new law that said the market belongs to the local people forever. And it still does.

london-bridge.name: London Bridge
london-bridge.angle: The old bridge is in America
london-bridge.story: This is the bridge next to the market. Everyone knows the name London Bridge, but most people imagine the wrong bridge. The one with the towers is Tower Bridge. This one looks simple, but it has a crazy story.
facts: There has been a bridge in this place for almost 2,000 years. The Romans built the first one. London grew up around it. The bridge you see now is made of concrete. It opened in 1973.

In the Middle Ages, London Bridge had houses and shops built on it. At one end, they put the heads of executed traitors on sticks, as a warning. In 1305, they put the head of William Wallace here. He was a real man, who led the Scots against the English king. The English caught him, called him a traitor, and executed him in London. In Scotland, he is a national hero. The film Braveheart is about him.

planCard.todo: Walk to the middle of the bridge. You can see Tower Bridge from there. At 9:20, go back to the market for breakfast. It's 3 minutes away.

london-bridge.onCamera: This is London Bridge. And no, it's not the one you're thinking of. The famous one with the towers is Tower Bridge, over there.
london-bridge.closeOnCamera: So where is the old London Bridge? In 1968, it was sold to an American businessman. He took it apart, shipped it to America, and built it again in the desert in Arizona. It's still there today. People say he thought he was buying Tower Bridge. He always said that wasn't true. But it's a good story.

borough-open.name: Borough Market — open
borough-open.angle: Breakfast in a very old market
borough-open.story: Come back to the market after London Bridge. Now it's open, busy and noisy. Have breakfast here. You filmed it empty, and now you can film it full.
facts: For most of the last century, this market was not for normal shoppers. Traders sold fruit and vegetables here in big boxes, to shops and restaurants. The food market you see today only started in 1998, with a food festival. People loved it so much that it opened every month, then every week, then every day.

Earlier, before the market opened, I told you how the local people bought it in the 1750s. They still own it today. A charity runs it for the local community. Not a company, and not the city council. Just like that old law promised.

see: The Globe pub on Bedale Street
planCard.todo: Have breakfast, about 20 minutes. Then walk east along the river to Tower Bridge. Leave by 9:40 for the 10:25 boat.

borough-open.onCamera: Same market, just half an hour later. Now it's open, it's busy, and it's time for breakfast.
borough-open.closeOnCamera: One more thing. See this street? It's called Stoney Street. In the Harry Potter films, it was the entrance to the Leaky Cauldron pub. And in the Bridget Jones films, her flat is above the pub on the corner. So you have probably seen this place before, without knowing it.

tower-bridge.name: Tower Bridge & the Tower of London
tower-bridge.angle: The bus that jumped the bridge
tower-bridge.story: A 15-minute walk along the river. This is the bridge most people think is London Bridge. Walk across it to the other side. The Tower of London is there, and so is the pier for your boat.
facts: Tower Bridge opened in 1894. It looks like an old castle, but inside the stone there is a steel frame. The middle of the road can lift up in two halves, so tall ships can pass under it. For 82 years, big steam engines lifted it.

Next to the bridge is the Tower of London. William the Conqueror started building it after he took over England in 1066. There's a famous legend: if the ravens, the big black birds, ever leave the Tower, the country will fall. But the Tower's own historian checked the old records. He found nothing about the ravens before the 1880s. So the legend is probably only about 140 years old. They still keep at least six ravens there, just in case.

routeCard.note: About 15 minutes' walk along the river from Borough Market.

planCard.todo: Walk over the bridge to the north side for the Tower of London. Then go down to Tower Pier. Be there by 10:20 for the 10:25 boat.

tower-bridge.onCamera: And this is the bridge everyone calls London Bridge. But it's not. This is Tower Bridge. And it's younger than it looks.
tower-bridge.closeOnCamera: But my favourite story about this bridge happened in December 1952. The bridge started to open while a red double-decker bus was on it. The driver, Albert Gunter, didn't stop. He drove faster, and the bus jumped across the gap. All twenty passengers were safe. He got ten pounds and a day off as a reward.

river-boat.name: The boat to Greenwich
river-boat.angle: Arrive by water, like people used to
river-boat.story: Get on the river boat at Tower Pier. Tap your bank card at the gate. Sit down for 20 minutes. When you get close to Greenwich, you will see two big matching buildings with a gap in the middle. That gap is the start of the next story.
facts: For most of London's history, the river was the main road. The streets were narrow, dirty and dangerous. So kings, goods and even coffins travelled by boat. Greenwich was built to be seen from the water.
These buildings were a home for old and injured sailors from the Royal Navy. It was called a hospital, but it was more like a big retirement home. Thousands of old sailors lived here.

routeCard.note: Uber Boat (Thames Clippers). Tap your bank card. About 20 minutes. Next boat 10:54.

see: The Naval College from the water
planCard.todo: Boat at 10:25 from Tower Pier. If you miss it, the next one is at 10:54. Sit on the right side to see Greenwich when you arrive.

river-boat.onCamera: No more walking. Now we take the river to Greenwich, the way people arrived here hundreds of years ago.
river-boat.closeOnCamera: Look how it's built: two halves, with a big gap in the middle. The architect was Christopher Wren, the same man who built St Paul's. Queen Mary the Second told him to leave that gap. That way, the small white house behind it, called the Queen's House, could still see the river.

painted-hall.name: The Painted Hall
painted-hall.angle: A dining room too fancy to eat in
painted-hall.story: A five-minute walk from the boat. This hall was built for old sailors to eat their meals. But it was so beautiful and so grand that they didn't want to eat there.
facts: The sailors felt uncomfortable eating in such a grand room. So they ate in the simple, dark room downstairs instead. They ate there for all the years it took to paint this hall.

In 1806, Admiral Nelson, Britain's most famous sailor, was killed at the Battle of Trafalgar. His body was brought here, and thousands of people came to say goodbye. Then his coffin went up the river by boat to St Paul's Cathedral, the one we saw this morning.

routeCard.note: 5 minutes' walk from Greenwich Pier. Open 10:00 to 5:00, last entry 4:30.

see: The Upper Hall at the far end
The undercroft where the sailors actually ate
planCard.todo: Look up first. Then walk to the far end of the hall. Leave at 11:40 for lunch.

painted-hall.onCamera: This room was built as a dining room for old sailors. But it came out so fancy that the sailors refused to eat in it.
painted-hall.closeOnCamera: Now look up. One painter, James Thornhill, painted all of this. It took him nineteen years, from 1707 to 1726. And he was paid by the size of the painting: three pounds for every square yard of ceiling, and one pound for the walls. This is what nineteen years of work looks like.

greenwich-lunch.name: Lunch, then up the hill
greenwich-lunch.story: Have lunch in Greenwich. Then walk up the hill in the park to the Observatory. It's steep. It takes about 15 minutes.

see: The view back down the hill
planCard.todo: Have lunch in Greenwich. Then walk up the hill in the park. It takes about 15 minutes. Be at the Observatory by 12:50 for the red ball.

time-ball.name: The Time Ball
time-ball.story: On the roof of the Observatory there is a big red ball on a pole. Every day, it drops at exactly one o'clock. It has done this since 1833.
facts: It was made for the ships on the River Thames. Before a long trip, the captain had to set the ship's clock exactly right. If the clock was wrong by even a few seconds, the ship could end up miles away from where it should be.
At five to one, the ball goes halfway up. At two minutes to one, it goes to the top. And at exactly one o'clock, it drops. It was one of the first public time signals in the world.

routeCard.sub: Royal Observatory · 12:55 PM · watch from outside
routeCard.note: Stand facing the red ball on the roof.

see: The red time ball on Flamsteed House
The view over London from the hilltop
planCard.todo: At 12:50, stand outside facing the red ball on the roof, and say your open. At 12:58 the ball goes to the top: say your close. At 1:00 it drops. If it's very windy, it won't work.

time-ball.onCamera: See that big red ball on the roof? Every day, at exactly one o'clock, it drops. It has done this every day since 1833.
time-ball.closeOnCamera: So why one o'clock, and not twelve? Because at twelve, the scientists here were busy. They were using their telescopes to check the time by the sun. So they dropped the ball an hour later, when they were free. And... here it goes.

observatory.name: The Royal Observatory
observatory.angle: The carpenter who beat the scientists
observatory.story: This is the biggest story of the day. For a long time, sailors could not tell exactly where they were at sea. Ships got lost and crashed. Parliament offered a huge prize to solve this. The top scientists looked at the stars. A carpenter built a clock. His clocks are here, and they still work.
facts: Sailors could tell how far north or south they were by looking at the sun. But they could not tell how far east or west they were. In 1707, some Navy ships got lost and crashed on rocks near the Isles of Scilly. More than a thousand sailors died. So Parliament offered a huge prize to anyone who could solve the problem.

Most scientists said the answer was in the stars. Harrison said the answer was a very good clock. The people in charge of the prize didn't like him. They kept changing the rules, and they didn't pay him. He was 80 years old before Parliament finally paid him, after the King himself helped him.

routeCard.note: Open until 6pm in September. It closes on 1 November 2026, until 2028.

planCard.todo: Start inside with Harrison's clocks, and say your open there. Then go out to the line on the ground, the meridian, and say your close. That's the end of Saturday. The Observatory closes on 1 November until 2028.

observatory.onCamera: These are the clocks of John Harrison. He was a carpenter, not a scientist. And with these clocks, he beat the best scientists in England. They still work today. This small one, H4, sailed to Jamaica in 1761. In 81 days, it was wrong by only five seconds.
observatory.closeOnCamera: And this is what it was all for. This line is zero degrees. One foot in the east, one foot in the west. The whole world measures east and west from this line. A carpenter, a clock, and a line around the planet. That's Greenwich.

highgate-cemetery.name: Highgate Cemetery
highgate-cemetery.story: In the 1800s, London had a big problem. The old churchyards were full of dead bodies. So new, big cemeteries were built on the edge of the city. Highgate was the most fashionable one. Rich and famous people were buried here.
facts: London's old churchyards were completely full. Old coffins were broken up to make space for new ones. People believed the smell caused disease. So private companies built seven big cemeteries around the edge of London. Highgate opened in 1839, and it became the fashionable place to be buried. Karl Marx, the man who wrote about communism, is buried here too.

Inside there is the Egyptian Avenue, a street of tombs that looks like ancient Egypt. At that time, the British were crazy about Egypt. It leads to a circle of family tombs, built around a huge old cedar tree. The tree was here before the cemetery. It went rotten inside, and in 2019 they had to cut it down. The young tree in the middle is the new one.

routeCard.note: Open 10:00 to 5:00, last entry 4:30. From Archway: 15 to 20 minutes uphill, or take a bus up Highgate Hill.

planCard.todo: Say your open at the gate on Swain's Lane. Inside, just film. The East side has Karl Marx. The West side has the Egyptian Avenue and the circle of tombs. Say your close back at the gate. If there is a funeral, move away.

highgate-cemetery.onCamera: By the 1830s, London had no more room to bury its dead. So they built this.
highgate-cemetery.closeOnCamera: One more story from inside. The painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti buried a book of his poems with his wife when she died. Seven years later, he changed his mind. He had her dug up at night, to get the poems back. But there's one story they don't allow me to tell in there. For that one, we're going across the road.

highgate-lunch.name: Lunch in Highgate village
highgate-lunch.story: Five minutes up the lane. Highgate still feels like a village.

planCard.todo: One hour for lunch. Then go to Waterlow Park, across the road from the cemetery.

waterlow-park.name: Waterlow Park
waterlow-park.angle: A garden for people with no garden
waterlow-park.story: The park is right across the road from the cemetery, and it's free. From the top, you can see all of London. This is where you tell the story the cemetery doesn't allow.
facts: This park was a gift. In 1889, Sir Sydney Waterlow, the Lord Mayor of London, gave all this land to the public. He called it a garden for people who don't have a garden. Back then, most people in London lived in crowded streets, with no garden at all.

The white house in the park is called Lauderdale House. It was built in 1582, before Shakespeare wrote his first play. People say that Nell Gwyn lived here. She was an actress, and the girlfriend of King Charles the Second.

routeCard.note: Right across the road from the cemetery.

planCard.todo: Go to the top terrace. Tell the vampire story there, with London behind you. Then say your close with the view. Walk down the hill at 2:15.

waterlow-park.onCamera: The cemetery doesn't allow this story inside, so I'll tell it here. In 1970, a newspaper wrote that a vampire lived in Highgate Cemetery. After that, crowds of people climbed over the walls at night, with wooden stakes and crosses, to hunt the vampire. The police had to stop them.
waterlow-park.closeOnCamera: From up here, you can see all of London. And at the bottom of this hill, there's a place from an old story. It's where a boy who was leaving London decided to turn back. That's where we're going next.

whittington-stone.name: The Whittington Stone
whittington-stone.story: Walk ten minutes down the hill. There is a stone with a cat on top. It marks a place from a famous English children's story, about a boy called Dick Whittington.
facts: Here is the story that every English child knows. Dick Whittington was a poor boy. He came to London because he heard the streets were made of gold. They weren't. He gave up and started to walk away, up this hill. Then he heard the bells. They seemed to say: turn back, Whittington, you will be Lord Mayor of London. So he went back. And in the story, his cat made him rich.

The stone was put here in 1821. The cat on top was added in 1964. The real Whittington had no children. When he died in 1423, he gave all his money to the city. It paid for homes for poor people, a library, a new prison, and one of the biggest public toilets in London.

routeCard.note: About 10 minutes' walk down the hill from Waterlow Park. Archway station is 2 minutes away.

see: The Whittington Stone and its cat
planCard.todo: The stone is on the pavement at the bottom of Highgate Hill. Archway tube station is at the bottom. Take the Northern line to Euston. It's about 10 minutes.

whittington-stone.onCamera: This is where, in the old story, a poor boy called Dick Whittington was leaving London. Here, he heard the church bells telling him to turn back. So he went back, and he became the Lord Mayor of London.
whittington-stone.closeOnCamera: But here's the surprise. The real Dick Whittington was not poor at all. His father was a knight. He became a very rich trader, and he lent money to kings. He was Lord Mayor of London four times, not three. And there was no cat.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
coldOpen.where: Westminster Bridge, 7am, when the city is still empty
facts: The hook: 'This is my first video in London. So I'm starting at seven in the morning, before the city wakes up.'
What this is: the famous places at sunrise, then two stories most tourists never hear.
The promise: a market the local people bought back, a carpenter who beat the scientists, and a hill where a boy leaving London turned back.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: the place where, in the story, a boy leaving London heard the bells and turned back.
The link: 'I came to see the famous places. But the best parts were the ones you won't find on a postcard.'
The ask: like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.

talkTipbox: Each stop has three parts. 1. OPEN: say it to the camera. 2. VOICEOVER: record it later, at home, over your video. 3. CLOSE: say it to the camera. You don't have to say it word for word. Use your own simple words. When you say a name, say who the person was.
goldenRules: Each stop: open on camera, voiceover later, close on camera.
Saturday has two fixed times: the 10:25 boat and the red ball at 1:00.
Borough Market opens at 9. Film the set-up from the street. Ask traders before you film them.
No tripod at Borough Market or Highgate. Hold the camera in your hand.
No ghost or vampire stories inside Highgate Cemetery. Tell that one in Waterlow Park.
It's a real cemetery. If there is a funeral, move away and stop filming.
Before you go: book the Observatory, the Painted Hall, Highgate and your train home.
outro: The famous places at sunrise, then the stories behind them. Have a good trip home.
